beats.narration_text: Last week this was a plan with nothing built. Now it has run. The question was easy to state and expensive to answer. Can one model, pretrained only on other people's Raman spectra, make our own bacteria classifiers better than training the same network from scratch? And if it can, what is the cheapest way to adapt it?

props.command: I pretrained one encoder on 242,156 public Raman spectra. Does it beat training from scratch on my two classification tasks, and is full fine-tuning or small adapters the better way to use it?
output: Compare four arms against a from-scratch control, five seeds each.

beats.narration_text: Short answer: yes. Starting from the pretrained model beats starting from scratch on both tasks. But the best way to use it depends on the task, one goal set in advance narrowly failed, and there is one class where pretraining made things worse.

props.text:
Yes, it helped.
On both tasks.

But how to use it
depends on the task.

beats.narration_text: Then four ways to use it, each with the same tuning budget. From scratch, as the control. Head only: freeze the pretrained model and train a new final layer. Full fine-tuning: start from it and train everything. And adapters: freeze it and train small add-on layers, four and a half percent of the parameters.

The first task: thirty bacterial isolates, tested on a separate measurement set. Full fine-tuning wins at eighty three point one, two point two points above scratch, with a confidence interval that excludes zero. Adapters land in between, and that gain cannot be told apart from zero. Head only comes last.

props.title: Thirty isolates, separate test set
props.caption: Test accuracy percent, mean of five seeds, bar is one sd

beats.narration_text: The second task is hard in a different way: five clinical classes, trained on 2018 data and tested on 2019. Here the adapters win, at ninety one point nine. That is four point one points above scratch and two point three above full fine-tuning, significant in all five seeds, while training about a twentieth of the parameters.

props.title: Five clinical classes, 2018 to 2019
props.caption: Test accuracy percent, mean of five seeds, bar is one sd

beats.narration_text: Why would the winner flip? Look at validation. Every arm scored around ninety four percent on the isolate task's validation, and around ninety nine on the clinical one. On test, seventy eight to ninety two. Validation came from the same files as training. The real difficulty is the shift between measurement sets and between years, and freezing the pretrained model acts as a brake that holds up best when the year changes.

lines: The hard part is the shift, not the classes.
meta: frozen weights hold up best when the year changes

beats.narration_text: One goal was set before any results. One shared base of twenty megabytes, plus an adapter of about one megabyte per task, and that adapter should land within one point of the best arm on both tasks. On the clinical task it was the best. On the isolate task it finished one point two three behind. The goal failed, by about a quarter of a point. It stays failed.

lines: One 20 MB base, a 1 MB adapter per task.
Goal: within 1 point of the best, both tasks.
Missed by 0.23 on one. It stays a miss.
meta: the threshold was written down before the results

beats.narration_text: And what this does not show. The base model was pretrained once, so run-to-run variation is unmeasured. Six of the eight learning rates landed at the edge of their grid, so some arms may be under-tuned, including the one that just missed. The scratch control used a schedule built for fine-tuning, which tilts slightly toward the pretrained start. And the test sets were scored exactly once.

Your turn. If you are choosing between fine-tuning a pretrained model and training small adapters, do not choose on validation alone. Here, validation was at a ceiling and could not separate them. Here is a prompt for testing against the shift you actually care about.

props.command: I have a pretrained encoder and two ways to adapt it: full fine-tuning or small adapters. My test data comes from a later time than my training data. How do I build a validation split that reflects that shift, so I can choose between them before touching the test set?

beats.narration_text: Did it help? Yes, and now we know where. Working notes from a Humanitarians AI fellowship. The failures are the part worth keeping.
